question: How many hydraulic systems are installed?

options.text: One, with three pumps
Two: A and B only
Three: A, B and standby
Four: A, B, C and D

explanation: Two full systems plus a limited third is what allows the primary controls to survive the loss of both main systems.

question: What is the normal operating pressure of the hydraulic systems?

options.text: 1500 psi
2000 psi
3000 psi
5000 psi

explanation: It is the standard pressure for transport aircraft of this generation, balancing actuator size against component weight.

question: How many pumps supply each main hydraulic system?

options.text: One: a single engine driven pump on each side
Two: an engine driven pump and an electric motor driven pump
Two: both of them driven by the engine gearbox
Three: two engine driven pumps and one electric motor pump

explanation: Two different types of pump means a failure of one power source does not remove the system.

question: Why is the electric pump for one system powered from the electrical bus on the opposite side?

options.text: So that the electrical load is shared evenly between the two main transfer buses in flight
Because the two pumps are mounted on opposite sides of the airplane structure
So that the pumps of one system can be started in sequence rather than together
So that a single electrical or engine failure does not remove both pumps of the same system

explanation: Cross powering breaks the link that would otherwise make one engine failure cost both pumps of one system.

question: How are the hydraulic reservoirs pressurised?

options.text: By bleed air
By an air compressor
By an accumulator
By gravity head

explanation: Positive pressure at the pump inlets prevents cavitation, particularly at altitude where the ambient pressure is low.

question: What is the consequence of losing reservoir pressurisation?

options.text: The pumps may cavitate and the system may overheat or fail
The fluid quantity indication becomes unreliable
The system reverts to the standby pump automatically
The reservoir overflows into the standby system

explanation: A pump drawing vapour instead of fluid delivers no pressure and damages itself in the process.

question: Which type of hydraulic fluid is used?

options.text: A fire resistant phosphate ester fluid
A water glycol based mixture
A silicone based synthetic fluid
A mineral based hydraulic oil

explanation: Fire resistance matters because the fluid is routed at high pressure near engines and electrical equipment.

question: Why is care taken to avoid skin and eye contact with the hydraulic fluid?

options.text: Because the fluid conducts electricity when it is warm
Because it degrades rapidly on contact with the air
Because the fluid is an irritant and can cause injury
Because the fluid is highly flammable at low pressure

explanation: The same chemistry that gives the fluid its fire resistance makes it aggressive to skin, eyes and some materials.

question: Which system normally powers the landing gear?

options.text: System B
The standby system
System A
Either, automatically

explanation: Knowing which system drives which user is what allows the crew to predict the consequences of a failure.

question: Which system normally powers the trailing edge flaps?

options.text: System A
Both systems together
The standby system
System B

explanation: Splitting the flaps and the leading edge devices between the two systems prevents one failure taking all the high lift devices.

question: Which system normally powers the leading edge devices?

options.text: System B
The standby system
The alternate drive
System A

explanation: With the trailing edge on the other system, a single hydraulic failure always leaves part of the high lift system available.

question: Which system powers the normal brakes?

options.text: System A
System B
The brake accumulator
The standby system

explanation: The alternate brake source is the other main system, so braking survives the loss of either one.

question: What supplies the brakes if the normal system is lost?

options.text: The standby hydraulic system through the rudder manifold
The alternate brake system on the other main hydraulic system
The nose wheel steering supply through a shuttle valve
The brake accumulator alone, until its charge is spent

explanation: The transfer happens without the airplane losing braking, although some functions such as antiskid behaviour may change.

question: Which system powers the nose wheel steering?

options.text: System A
System B
The standby system
An electric actuator

explanation: Loss of that system means steering must be achieved by differential braking and thrust at low speed.

question: Which hydraulic sources can operate the thrust reversers?

options.text: The main systems and the standby system
The main systems and the brake accumulator
The standby system and the accumulator
The main hydraulic systems only

explanation: Reverse thrust is retained after a hydraulic failure because the standby system can operate the reversers.

question: What does the standby hydraulic system power?

options.text: The rudder, the leading edge devices in extension, and the thrust reversers
The trailing edge flaps, the spoilers and the landing gear retraction
All of the primary flight controls, in place of the main systems
The landing gear, the brakes and the nose wheel steering system

explanation: It is a limited system providing exactly what is needed to keep the airplane controllable and stoppable.

question: How is the standby system powered?

options.text: By an air driven pump using bleed air
By an engine driven pump on engine 1
By an electric motor driven pump
By a ram air turbine deployed in flight

explanation: Its independence from the engines is what makes it available after the loss of both engine driven pumps.

question: Does the standby system have its own reservoir?

options.text: No, it draws from the system A reservoir
No, it draws from the system B reservoir
Yes, it is supplied from a separate reservoir
No, it shares a common reservoir with both systems

explanation: A separate fluid supply means a leak that empties a main system does not empty the standby system as well.

question: How can the standby system be brought into operation?

options.text: Automatically on loss of the main systems only, with no manual selection available to the crew at all
Manually from the flight control switches only, with no automatic operation at all
Manually by selecting the alternate flap master switch only, with no other path
Automatically on loss of the main systems, or manually by the flight control or alternate flap selections

explanation: Several paths exist because the system is needed in several different failure cases.

question: What does a hydraulic pump LOW PRESSURE light indicate?

options.text: That pump switch has been left in the OFF position
The reservoir quantity for that system is low
That pump is not producing its normal output pressure
That system has overheated and shut itself down

explanation: It refers to the individual pump, which is why the system pressure indication must be read alongside it.

question: What does an electric pump OVERHEAT light indicate?

options.text: The reservoir pressurisation for that system has failed
The pump or its fluid has reached an excessive temperature
The system pressure has exceeded its normal limit
The pump has been running with the system unpressurised

explanation: An overheating pump is usually working against a restriction or running with insufficient fluid, and continuing will destroy it.

question: Why is a low reservoir quantity more serious than a low pressure indication?

options.text: Because a low quantity disables the standby system as well as that one
Because the pumps cannot be switched off once the quantity is low
Because the quantity indication drives the pressure indication
Because it suggests fluid is being lost and the system cannot be restored

explanation: Pressure can be lost and regained, but fluid that has left the airplane is not coming back.

question: What is the purpose of the power transfer unit?

options.text: It pressurises the reservoirs of both systems from the hydraulic pumps rather than from bleed air
It transfers fluid between the two main reservoirs to equalise their quantities
It uses pressure from one system to provide hydraulic power in the other without transferring fluid
It connects the standby system to both main systems when either one fails

explanation: Transferring power rather than fluid means the two systems stay isolated even while one supports the other.

question: Why does the power transfer unit not transfer fluid between systems?

options.text: Because contamination or a leak in one system would then affect the other
Because the two reservoirs are held at two quite different pressures
Because the fluids used in the two systems are not the same
Because transferring fluid would unbalance the airplane laterally

explanation: The whole value of having two systems rests on them being independent, and shared fluid would destroy that independence.

question: Which functions does the power transfer unit typically support?

options.text: The leading edge devices and the autoslat function
The normal brake system and the antiskid
The nose wheel steering and the tiller
The landing gear retraction and its doors sequence

explanation: It exists to preserve the high lift and stall protection functions when their normal source is lost.

question: What is the purpose of the landing gear transfer unit?

options.text: It transfers the operation of the landing gear to the standby hydraulic system when a pump is unavailable
It allows the landing gear to be extended manually when the normal hydraulic source has been lost
It isolates the landing gear system from the manifold once the gear has been retracted and locked
It provides the volume needed to retract the gear at the normal rate when an engine driven pump is unavailable

explanation: Gear retraction is a high volume demand, and losing an engine at the worst moment is exactly when it still has to happen quickly.

question: What does the hydraulic system pressure indication show?

options.text: The brake accumulator pressure
The pressure available in each system
The reservoir pressurisation pressure
The output of each individual pump

explanation: System pressure is what the users actually see, regardless of which pump is producing it.

question: What is the purpose of the brake accumulator?

options.text: It supplies the standby hydraulic system whenever its electric pump has been switched off
It pressurises the brake system reservoir so the pumps do not cavitate
It stores pressure for the parking brake and provides a limited number of brake applications
It smooths the output of the brake system pump and damps the pressure surges

explanation: It is what allows the parking brake to hold with no system running and gives some braking after a total hydraulic loss.

question: Why is the accumulator pressure checked before flight?

options.text: Because it indicates how much fluid is remaining in that system reservoir
Because it determines the maximum brake temperature that is allowed
Because it must be discharged before the landing gear is retracted
Because it is the reserve for parking and for braking after a hydraulic failure

explanation: A reserve that has leaked down is worthless in exactly the situation it exists for.

question: What is the effect of losing hydraulic system A alone?

options.text: The standby system takes over all of the system A functions at once
The primary controls remain powered but several individual users are lost
The airplane cannot be landed with any flap setting selected
All of the flight controls revert to manual reversion at once

explanation: The primary surfaces are dual supplied, and the cost of the failure is in the configuration changing systems.

question: What is the effect of losing hydraulic system B alone?

options.text: The primary controls remain powered and the trailing edge flaps require the alternate drive
The rudder reverts to the standby system immediately and the flaps become unavailable
The nose wheel steering is unaffected and the landing gear extends normally
The landing gear cannot be extended and the manual system must be used

explanation: Each main system loss produces a different list of affected users, which is why the two failures are not interchangeable.

question: What is the effect of losing both main hydraulic systems?

options.text: All of the flight controls are lost and the airplane can no longer be controlled in any axis
The primary controls revert to manual reversion except the rudder, which uses the standby system
The standby system powers all of the primary flight controls on its own
The airplane is controllable only through the stabiliser trim and the thrust

explanation: Understanding what remains is what makes the situation survivable, since the airplane is still controllable but very different to fly.

question: How are the landing gear extended if system A is lost?

options.text: By the system B pumps through the landing gear transfer unit
By the manual extension system, allowing the gear to free fall
By the standby hydraulic system through the rudder manifold
By the power transfer unit driving the retract actuators

explanation: Gravity and the unlocking of the uplocks are enough to get the gear down, which is why no second hydraulic source is needed.

question: Why are the engine driven pumps normally left on throughout the flight?

options.text: Because they cannot be switched off in any way once the engines have been started and stabilised
Because the electric pumps are unable to supply the full flow the system needs
Because switching them off would depressurise the reservoirs of both systems
Because they are the primary source and the electric pumps are there to supplement and back them up

explanation: The architecture assumes both pumps of a system are available, and turning one off deliberately reduces the margin.

question: What is the purpose of the hydraulic system quantity indication?

options.text: It shows the temperature of the fluid in each system
It shows the fluid remaining in each reservoir
It shows the output of each of the electric pumps
It shows the pressure available in each system

explanation: Quantity is the measure of whether the system still has what it needs to keep working.

question: Why might a hydraulic quantity indication read low without a leak?

options.text: Because the fluid contracts at low temperature and nothing else
Because the pumps retain some of the fluid when switched off
Because the reservoir pressurisation compresses the fluid a little
Because fluid is held in the actuators when some systems are extended

explanation: Fluid in an extended actuator is out of the reservoir, so the indication depends on the configuration of the airplane.

question: Why is a rapid decrease in quantity treated differently from a slow one?

options.text: Because a slow loss indicates that a pump has failed internally
Because a rapid loss triggers the standby system automatically
Because a rapid loss indicates an active leak that may empty the system
Because the indication is accurate only above a minimum quantity

explanation: The rate of loss is what determines whether there is time to reach a destination or whether the system must be isolated.

question: What is the value of switching off a pump in a system that is losing fluid?

options.text: It transfers the affected users over to the other system
It isolates the reservoir from the leak in the system
It restores the system pressure to its normal value
It can slow the loss and protect the pump from running dry

explanation: Reducing the flow through the leak buys time, and a pump running without fluid will fail and may become an ignition source.

question: Which flight control surface can be powered by all three hydraulic sources?

options.text: The ailerons
The elevators
The spoilers
The rudder

explanation: Directional control after an engine failure cannot be obtained manually, which justifies the third source.

question: Why are the spoiler panels divided between the two main systems?

options.text: So that the inboard and outboard panels can move at different rates
So that the autobrake system can control the panels separately
So that a single hydraulic failure leaves some spoiler function available
So that the peak hydraulic demand on either system is reduced

explanation: Distributing the users is a recurring principle, and it turns a total loss of a function into a partial one.

question: What is the relationship between the hydraulic and the pneumatic systems?

options.text: Bleed air drives the standby hydraulic pump
Hydraulic pressure drives the bleed air valves
Bleed air pressurises the hydraulic reservoirs
The systems share a common heat exchanger

explanation: The dependence means a bleed problem can become a hydraulic problem, which is not obvious from the panel layout.

question: What is the relationship between the hydraulic and the electrical systems?

options.text: The hydraulic system generates electrical power through the transfer unit
The electric pumps and the standby pump depend on electrical power
The two systems are entirely independent of each other in flight
The hydraulic pumps drive the generators through the accessory gearbox

explanation: A total electrical failure therefore leaves only the engine driven pumps, which is a consideration in a multiple failure case.

question: Why does the loss of one engine not remove a complete hydraulic system?

options.text: Because each system also has an electric pump powered independently of that engine
Because the power transfer unit simply replaces the pump that has just been lost
Because the remaining engine drives both of the engine driven pumps
Because the standby system takes over that system automatically

explanation: Losing an engine costs one pump in one system, not the system itself.

question: What is checked on the hydraulic panel before flight?

options.text: Pump switch positions, system pressures and reservoir quantities
Fluid type, filter condition and the reservoir quantities
Accumulator charging rate, pressures and fluid temperatures
Power transfer unit operation and the system pressures

explanation: The panel shows whether both systems are complete and pressurised, which is the assumption every later procedure rests on.

question: Why is a hydraulic failure often described as a configuration problem rather than a control problem?

options.text: Because the flight controls have an electrical backup that the other systems simply do not have
Because the primary controls remain powered while the gear, flaps, brakes and steering are affected
Because hydraulic failures occur mostly during a change of configuration in flight
Because the airplane becomes uncontrollable only once it is back on the ground

explanation: The airplane still flies, and the difficulty appears when it has to be configured, landed and stopped.
